primary_meaning: God’s righteous evaluation of human persons, deeds, peoples, or powers, resulting in a just verdict—vindication or condemnation—and often in reward, punishment, or separation. In Christian teaching, “judgment” most commonly points especially to the final, eschatological judgment by God through Christ.
primary_basis: Ecclesiastes 12:14 — God brings every deed, including hidden things, into judgment.
Matthew 25:31–46 — the Son of Man separates the righteous from the wicked and assigns their respective destinies.
John 5:22–29 — the Father entrusts judgment to the Son, followed by resurrection to life or judgment.
Acts 17:31 — God has appointed a day to judge the world in righteousness through the risen Christ.
Romans 2:5–16 — God’s impartial judgment assesses deeds and hidden things.
2 Corinthians 5:10 — all appear before Christ’s judgment seat to receive according to what they have done.
Revelation 20:11–15 — the dead are judged before the great white throne according to their deeds.

alternatives.meaning: Historical or temporal divine judgment: God acts within history against individuals, nations, cities, or oppressive powers through disaster, defeat, exile, or societal collapse.

Condemnation or punitive sentence specifically, rather than the whole neutral process of evaluation. In many passages “judgment” functions almost synonymously with adverse verdict, wrath, or destruction.
Disciplinary, corrective, or purifying judgment directed toward God’s people, intended to expose sin, produce repentance, or restore holiness rather than merely condemn.
Vindication and deliverance: judgment is good news for the oppressed because God condemns evil, establishes justice, and publicly vindicates the faithful.
Moral discernment or self-examination by believers, including distinguishing right from wrong and assessing oneself before God.

notes: There is broad consensus on the core meaning of divine evaluation and just verdict, especially in relation to final judgment. However, “judgment” is not a symbol with one rigid referent in every passage: context determines whether it emphasizes evaluation, condemnation, temporal punishment, discipline, separation, or vindication.
